extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, judges, legislators, and policy-makers
extracted.subtask_description: Normative and doctrinal guidance on structuring administrative agencies, dividing agency powers (legislative/executive/judicial), and tailoring judicial review and statutory design accordingly. Includes a proposed statute to rework independent commissions' enforcement leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential removal power for executive officers
rubrics_metrics.description: When an officer performs properly executive functions, Myers governs and the President must have plenary removal power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humphrey’s Executor permits for-cause protection where duties are 'neither political nor executive, but predominantly quasi-judicial and quasi-legislative.' But for properly executive functions (e.g., enforcement commissioners exercising executive power), the President constitutionally controls them and should have plenary removal authority. The article contrasts Myers (executive officers) and Humphrey’s (independent commissions) and notes Morrison’s modification focusing on whether removal restrictions impede the President’s ability to perform constitutional duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design independent commission leadership as presidentially removable chief commissioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent commissions with enforcement authority should have chief commissioners appointed by the President with Senate advice and consent and subject to presidential removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed Independent Commission Reform Act text adapts 28 U.S.C. § 541: (a) presidential appointment with Senate advice/consent; (b) four-year term with holdover until successor qualifies; (c) subject to removal by the President; (d) duty to prosecute offenses and civil actions to extent permitted by the commission’s statute. The statute can adapt §§ 542-550 for oaths, vacancies, etc., and narrow commissioners' duties compared to U.S. Attorneys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate judicial review by the kind of administrative power
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial review should vary explicitly depending on whether the agency function is legislative (rulemaking), executive (enforcement), or judicial (adjudication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article argues the current appellate model implicitly differentiates functions but courts should make explicit distinctions so the nature of review corresponds to the constitutional branch analog. For rulemaking, courts should use full statutory-interpretation tools and defer only as a last resort; enforcement actions are executive and less amenable to judicial review of prosecutorial decisions; adjudications implicating private rights may require Article III scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit Chevron deference; use full tools of statutory interpretation first
rubrics_metrics.description: When agencies promulgate rules, courts should deploy all traditional tools of statutory construction (text, context, intent, purpose, history, background principles, conventions) before deferring to an agency's interpretation; deference (Chevron) should be a last resort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because agencies may be 'making law' rather than merely interpreting it, the same interpretive rigor used when courts review congressional action should apply. Courts should ensure Congress actually intended to delegate the lawmaking power in question and should limit delegation where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat agency-made law with scrutiny comparable to congressional enactments
rubrics_metrics.description: If agencies are making law, courts ought to review those laws with the same level of scrutiny as they do congressional enactments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article parallels the Constitution–Congress relationship with statutes–agencies and argues for similar methods of interpretation to determine the existence and scope of delegation. This supports limiting delegation to only what Congress truly granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement nonreviewability principle (Heckler) for prosecutorial discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency's refusal to initiate enforcement proceedings is presumptively unreviewable and is at the core of executive discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heckler v. Chaney establishes that nonenforcement decisions are typically not subject to judicial review because they are executive in nature; constitutional administration respects this separation and treats enforcement-inaction as part of presidential discretion under the Take Care Clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater (though still deferential) reviewability for denials of petitions for rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency refusals to initiate rulemaking are more susceptible to judicial review than refusals to enforce because they are less frequent, involve legal analysis, are subject to formalities, and often follow a procedural right to petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Massachusetts v. EPA distinguishes rulemaking denials as involving public explanation and legal issues; courts review such denials but the review is described as 'extremely limited' and 'highly deferential.' Constitutional administration treats rulemaking inaction like other legislative-context actions—first exhaust interpretive tools, then defer only if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate model of administrative review (generally non-de novo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial review of agency action is essentially appellate in nature: it ensures agencies considered appropriate factors rather than rehearing matters de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even many adjudicative administrative decisions do not receive de novo review in Article III courts; cases like Crowell and Atlas Roofing illustrate that agencies may make factual determinations that are final unless constitutional rights are implicated. The review ensures consideration of appropriate factors, and the 'hard look' test is used to detect arbitrariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'hard look' review to check arbitrary or capricious agency actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts employ the 'hard look' test to determine if an agency's actions are arbitrary or capricious, serving primarily as a spur to agency use of expertise rather than as full de novo review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hard-look standard (e.g., Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm) compels agencies to rely on expertise and reasoned decision-making; it is part of the deferential judicial toolkit for reviewing technical factual and policy determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defer to agency expertise on technical factual and policy matters
rubrics_metrics.description: When matters of fact and technical policy are at issue, courts generally defer to an agency's expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases like Baltimore Gas demonstrate that courts should be most deferential when scientific or technical determinations are involved; this is balanced against textual and other interpretive tools when statutory or constitutional questions arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article III protection and de novo review for core private rights adjudications
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters that deprive individuals of life, liberty, or core private property rights—historically the subject of Article III adjudication—require de novo review by Article III courts when adjudicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recommends adopting the bankruptcy model: when private rights are at stake, agency judges (e.g., ALJs) should issue reports and recommendations for de novo review by Article III judges. Cases like Northern Pipeline and Stern underscore the need to protect traditional judicial power in these contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit delegation doctrine: courts should construe delegations narrowly
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegation of lawmaking authority is constitutionally suspect; courts should limit delegations and permit only as much as Congress truly intended to grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because delegation is, as an original matter, unconstitutional, courts should exhaust statutory-interpretation tools to determine the scope of delegation and minimize judicially endorsed transfers of lawmaking power to agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional review and political accountability in constitutional administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional administration preserves Congress’s power to review and mark up agency rulemakings, reducing the need for direct presidential directive control for political accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By allowing Congress to review agency rulemakings after agencies provide recommendations, constitutional administration can enhance technocratic decision-making and accountability without requiring direct presidential administration of rulemaking functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural statutory design for commissioners' duties and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory design of commissioners should clearly define and narrow duties (e.g., omitting many U.S. Attorneys’ duties except prosecuting offenses and civil actions), aligning their authority with constitutional constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed statute adopts U.S. Attorneys’ statutory form but narrows duties (omit §547 duties like defending the United States in actions), tailors prosecutorial responsibilities to each commission’s jurisdiction, and houses adjudication within the administrative apparatus with appropriate Article III review for traditional common-law rights.
